proofs.main:
Existence of the isotropic pair: in the orthonormal basis of the section “Setting and imports” take
\begin{align*}
w_1 &:= a_1 + b_1, & w_2 &:= a_2 + b_2, & w_3 &:= b_3 + i\,b_4,\\
w_1' &:= \tfrac12(a_1 - b_1), & w_2' &:= \tfrac12(a_2 - b_2), & w_3' &:= -\tfrac12(b_3 - i\,b_4).
\end{align*}
The first two isotropic vectors pair a plus direction with a minus direction and are real; the third pairs two minus directions and is complex, $Q(b_3 + ib_4) = -1 + 1 = 0$; and $\ip{w_j}{w_k'} = \delta_{jk}$, $\ip{w_j}{w_k} = \ip{w_j'}{w_k'} = 0$ by inspection. This is the basis the verification script uses, over the Gaussian rationals. Conjugacy: two dual pairs $(W, W')$ and $(U, U')$ with dual bases $w_j, w_j'$ and $u_j, u_j'$ have the same Gram matrix $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & I \\ I & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, so the linear map $w_j \mapsto u_j$, $w_j' \mapsto u_j'$ is an isometry of $V_\C$ carrying one pair to the other. The Clifford relation: for $w_1, w_2 \in W$, $\{w_1\wedge, w_2\wedge\} = 0$ and $\ip{w_1}{w_2} = 0$; for $w'_1, w'_2 \in W'$ likewise with $\{\iota_{w'_1}, \iota_{w'_2}\} = 0$; and the mixed case is the graded Leibniz identity: contraction is the degree $-1$ derivation extending $\iota_{w'}(w) = \ip{w}{w'}$, so for $\xi \in \Lambda^k W$,
\[
\iota_{w'}(w\wedge\xi) = \ip{w}{w'}\,\xi - w\wedge\iota_{w'}\xi, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \{w\wedge, \iota_{w'}\} = \ip{w}{w'}\,\id ,
\]
which the script also verifies on every basis state. Expanding $u = w + w'$,
\[
c(u)^2 = 2\,(w\wedge + \iota_{w'})^2 = 2\,\{w\wedge, \iota_{w'}\} = 2\ip{w}{w'}\,\id = Q(u)\,\id ,
\]
using $Q(w+w') = 2\ip{w}{w'}$. Since $\Cl(V_\C) = T(V_\C)/\langle u\otimes u - Q(u)\rangle$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complex-clifford-algebra}(i), the complex form of \claimref{std-algebra.existence-uniqueness}), a linear map $c: V_\C \to A$ into an algebra with $c(u)^2 = Q(u)1$ factors uniquely through $\Cl(V_\C)$; so $c$ extends. Isomorphism: $\Cl(V_\C)$ is spanned by the $64$ ordered products of the six basis vectors (the Clifford relations reorder any word into one of them; \claimref{std-algebra.complex-clifford-algebra}(i)), and the script checks that their $64$ images are linearly independent in $\End(\Lambda^\bullet W)$; so $c$ is injective on a spanning set of size $64 = \dim \End(\Lambda^\bullet W)$, hence bijective, and $\Cl(V_\C) \cong \End(\C^8)$ is simple. Irreducibility and uniqueness: $\End(\C^8)$ acts irreducibly on $\C^8$ (any nonzero vector is carried onto any other by a rank-one map), and every module $M$ of a full matrix algebra is a direct sum of copies of $\C^8$: the matrix units give $M = \bigoplus_i E_{ii}M$ with $E_{1i}: E_{ii}M \to E_{11}M$ and $E_{i1}$ inverse isomorphisms, so $M \cong \C^8 \otimes E_{11}M$, and an irreducible $M$ is $\C^8$. Vectors are odd operators (wedge and contraction each shift exterior degree by one), so the even subalgebra preserves the parity split, and on an 8-dimensional module with a 4+4 split the even part $\Cl^0(V_\C)$, of dimension 32, maps onto $\End(\CS)\oplus\End(\CSm)$, of dimension $16 + 16 = 32$, injectively by simplicity of its two factors and the disjointness of their supports; the script checks the block structure exactly.

correspondence.googly-localisation-quart.formal: There is a palatial construction (a deformation of the holomorphic function algebra of the conformal spinor space $\CS$ (twistor space) within $\mathcal{P}$, in the programme of \cite{Penrose15}) with the following two parts. \emph{(a)} Anti-self-dual (nonlinear graviton) curvature data enters at the commutative level: the construction restricted to the ASD sector reduces, at order $\hbar^0$, to the deformed projective spinor spaces (Penrose's curved twistor spaces) of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-nonlinear-graviton}, and its ASD data is insensitive to operator ordering, the consistency of which is Proposition \claimref{correspondence.chirality-split-ordering-insensitivity-asd-sector}(2). \emph{(b)} The self-dual, googly data is carried \emph{exactly} by the quartic-order ordering tensor of Lemma \claimref{correspondence.ordering-filtration}: the $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$-valued discrepancy assignments $(M, N) \mapsto$ (reordering defect of $q(M)q(N)$-words in the deformed product), which by Lemma \claimref{correspondence.ordering-filtration}(3) lie precisely where curvature operators lie. In particular the googly information resides not in ordering ambiguities generically but at quartic order specifically.
correspondence.googly-localisation-quart.technical:
Conjecture. There is a palatial construction, a deformation of the holomorphic function algebra of the conformal spinor space inside the palatial algebra $\mathcal{P}$ in Penrose's programme, with two features. Restricted to the anti-self-dual sector it reduces at order $\hbar^0$ to the deformed projective spinor spaces of the nonlinear graviton, and its anti-self-dual data is insensitive to operator ordering, consistently with the proved ordering insensitivity of that sector.

The self-dual, googly data is carried exactly by the quartic-order ordering tensor: the $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$-valued reordering defects of $q(M)q(N)$-words in the deformed product, which by the ordering filtration lie where curvature operators lie. So the googly information would reside at quartic order specifically, not in ordering ambiguities generically.
correspondence.googly-localisation-quart.lay: Penrose's nonlinear graviton captures one half of the gravitational field strength, the anti-self-dual Weyl half, through a curved version of the projective spinor space of the conformal algebra; the other half is called the googly data. This conjecture proposes that, in a noncommutative version of that construction (Penrose's palatial programme), the anti-self-dual half is untouched by questions of operator ordering, while the googly half is carried precisely by the ordering effects that first appear when four of its operators are multiplied. It is a proposal, not a proved result.
correspondence.googly-localisation-quart.typing_note: Conjecture with its existing motivated_by lineage kept; no edges.

correspondence.imported-complete-reducib.formal: Every finite-dimensional representation of $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\C)$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations, and the decomposition of a representation into isotypic components (the sum of all subrepresentations isomorphic to a given irreducible) is canonical. \emph{Provenance:} Weyl's complete reducibility theorem, e.g.\ \cite[\S6.3, \S7]{Humphreys72}.
correspondence.imported-complete-reducib.technical: Weyl's complete reducibility theorem for $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\C)$: every finite-dimensional representation $U$ is a direct sum of irreducible representations. Its isotypic components, each the sum of all subrepresentations isomorphic to a given irreducible, are canonical, so the decomposition $U = \bigoplus_\lambda U_\lambda$ into isotypic parts does not depend on any choices.
correspondence.imported-complete-reducib.lay: A standard theorem about symmetries says that any finite-dimensional representation of the basic symmetry algebra $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\C)$ breaks apart cleanly into irreducible building blocks. Grouping together the blocks of the same type gives a decomposition that does not depend on any choices. The result is imported from the textbook literature.

imported_from.citation: J. E. Humphreys, Introduction to Lie Algebras and Representation Theory, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 9, Springer (1972).

correspondence.imported-nonlinear-gravit.formal: For a complex $4$-manifold with anti-self-dual (half-flat) vacuum conformal structure, the $\alpha$-plane distribution defined fibrewise by the ruling of the Klein quadric is integrable; the leaf space of the resulting foliation is a complex $3$-manifold, the \emph{curved twistor space}; spacetime points reappear as rational curves with normal bundle $\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(1)$; and the conformal structure is recovered from curve intersection. Conversely such a curved twistor space determines the half-flat spacetime. \emph{Provenance:} \cite{Penrose76}. In the language of this paper: half-flatness is exactly the condition under which the completion's point space, the fibrewise Klein quadric of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.spinor-identification}, globalises to a deformed projective spinor space with the incidence dictionary of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart} intact. \emph{Beyond one flat chart.} The complex four-manifold with its half-flat conformal structure, and the curved twistor space as the leaf space of its $\alpha$-plane foliation, are global and are not carried by a single gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}). Even the pointwise condition needs the complex setting: the Weyl map $\mathcal{W}$ of a real field is linear over $\{1, I\}$ with $I^{2} = -1$, so a nonzero $\mathcal{W}$ of one handedness only exists for a complexified field, and the statement is read on the complex manifold, whose half-flatness is that condition on the Weyl part of its curvature.
correspondence.imported-nonlinear-gravit.technical:
Penrose's nonlinear graviton: on a complex $4$-manifold with anti-self-dual (half-flat) vacuum conformal structure, the $\alpha$-plane distribution given fibrewise by the ruling of the Klein quadric is integrable. Its leaf space is a complex $3$-manifold, Penrose's curved twistor space, in which spacetime points reappear as rational curves with normal bundle $\mathcal{O}(1)\oplus\mathcal{O}(1)$, and the conformal structure is recovered from how these curves intersect. Conversely such a curved twistor space determines the half-flat spacetime.

In the language of the series, half-flatness is exactly the condition under which the completion's point space, the fibrewise Klein quadric of the spinor identification, globalises to a deformed projective spinor space with the incidence dictionary intact. Its complex half-flat four-manifold and curved twistor space are global: no single gravitational field on flat spacetime carries them, so that part is read on complexified charts (holomorphic gauge fields on open sets of $\C^{4}$) glued by holomorphic gauge transformations, the twistor space being the leaf space of their $\alpha$-plane foliation.
correspondence.imported-nonlinear-gravit.lay: Penrose showed that a complex spacetime whose vacuum curvature has one handedness only (anti-self-dual, or half-flat) can be encoded in a curved three-dimensional complex space, a deformation of the projective spinor space of the conformal algebra. Points of spacetime become curves in that space, and the spacetime geometry can be read back from how those curves meet; the construction also runs in reverse. Here it is quoted as an established result and restated in the series' language.

imported_from.citation: R. Penrose, Nonlinear gravitons and curved twistor theory, Gen. Relativ. Gravit. 7 (1976), 31--52.

correspondence.incidence-relation-chart.formal:
Fix bases $\pi_1, \pi_2$ of $\Spi$ and $e_1, e_2$ of $\Som$ with $\pi_1\wedge\pi_2 = N_0$ and $e_1 \wedge e_2 = N_\infty$. For a linear map $A: \Spi \to \Som$ let $L_A := \{A\pi + \pi : \pi \in \Spi\}$ be its graph line and
\[
P(A) \;:=\; (A\pi_1 + \pi_1)\wedge(A\pi_2 + \pi_2) \;\in\; \Lambda^2\CS
\]
its Pl\"ucker bivector, normalised by $P(0) = N_0$. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item \emph{(Expansion.)} $P(A) = N_0 + \varphi(A) + (\det A)\, N_\infty$, where $\varphi(A) := A\pi_1\wedge\pi_2 + \pi_1\wedge A\pi_2$ lies in the mixed slot $\Som\wedge\Spi$ and $\det$ is taken in the chosen bases.
\item \emph{(The chart, term by term.)} $\varphi$ is a linear isomorphism onto the mixed slot $= \{\nO,\nInf\}^\perp \otimes \C$, and satisfies $Q(\varphi(A)) = -2\det A$. Writing $m(A) := \varphi(A)$ as a vector of $\{\nO,\nInf\}^\perp\otimes\C$, the Pl\"ucker bivector is exactly the completion's point embedding, complexified:
\[
P(A) \;=\; \nO \,+\, m(A)\,-\,\tfrac12\,Q(m(A))\,\nInf \;=\; X\bigl(m(A)\bigr).
\]
In particular every $P(A)$ is null, as a Pl\"ucker bivector must be, and the nullity of $P(A)$ is equivalent to the identity $\det A = -\tfrac12Q(m(A))$: the quadratic term of the chart is a determinant.
\item \emph{(Coverage.)} $A \mapsto L_A$ is a bijection from $\operatorname{Hom}(\Spi, \Som)$ onto the lines of $\PCS$ skew to $L_\infty$, and $[P(A)]$ ranges exactly over the points of the Klein quadric with $\ip{P}{\nInf} \neq 0$: the affine chart of the complexified conformal compactification, with the lines meeting $L_\infty$ as the points at infinity; the real locus is cut out in Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(5).
\item \emph{(Consequences.)} (i) The null pair adjoined by the Witt completion is the pair of skew lines $(L_\infty, L_0)$ (Proposition \claimref{correspondence.skew-lines-splittings-hyperbolic-planes-one}). (ii) The splitting of a conformal spinor (a twistor) into its $(\omega, \pi)$ parts along $\CS = \Som\oplus\Spi$ is the Witt completion seen at spinor level: the same datum in a third language. (iii) The incidence relation (Penrose's $\omega = ix\pi$; in the real algebra $\omega = \tfrac12 x\,\nInf\,\pi$, real-linear in $x$) is the case $A = I_6\hat x$ of the chart map, with $I_6$ the complex unit of $\CS$ (a factor of $i$: with $I_6 = e_0e_1e_2e_3e_4e_5$, $I_6$ acts as $-i$ on $\CS$) and $\hat x$ Hermitian for the invariant Hermitian form $\Sigma$ (the twistor form) of Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(5)). (iv) The stabiliser of the infinity line $L_\infty$ in $\mathfrak{so}(V_\C)$ is the stabiliser of the ray of $\nInf$: the Poincar\'e parabolic, with its Levi factor acting on $\Som \oplus \Spi$ as the two chiral $2$-dimensional representations, one plane the doublet of each $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\C)$ factor of the complexified Lorentz algebra and trivial for the other (Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chiral-planes-summand-spaces}(1)).
\end{enumerate}
correspondence.incidence-relation-chart.lay: Penrose described a spacetime point by a line in a three-dimensional complex projective space, through his incidence relation. This theorem shows that, written out term by term, the coordinates of that line are exactly the null vector by which the completed algebra represents the point, so the incidence relation is the completion's coordinate chart. The quadratic term of the chart is a determinant, the lines meeting a fixed line at infinity are the points at infinity, and the symmetries fixing that line are those of flat spacetime.

proofs.main:
(1) Expand bilinearly. The $\pi_1\wedge\pi_2$ term is $N_0$. The cross terms give $\varphi(A)$, manifestly in $\Som\wedge\Spi$. The top term is $A\pi_1\wedge A\pi_2$, a bivector of the $2$-plane $\Som$, hence a multiple of $e_1\wedge e_2$; writing $A\pi_i = \sum_j A_{ji}e_j$, the multiple is $A_{11}A_{22} - A_{21}A_{12} = \det A$.
(2) $P(A)$ is decomposable by construction, hence null (Theorem \claimref{correspondence.spinor-identification}(2)). Expanding its norm with Proposition \claimref{correspondence.skew-lines-splittings-hyperbolic-planes-one} (the mixed slot is orthogonal to the hyperbolic plane):
\[
0 \;=\; Q(P(A)) \;=\; Q(\varphi(A)) + 2\det A\,\ip{N_0}{N_\infty}
 \;=\; Q(\varphi(A)) + 2\det A ,
\]
which is the displayed norm identity, and equivalently $\det A = -\tfrac12Q(m(A))$; substituting back into (1) yields $P(A) = X(m(A))$ exactly, in the chart normalisation of the section “Setting and imports”. Injectivity of $\varphi$: if $\varphi(A) = 0$ then $P(A) = N_0 + (\det A)N_\infty$ is decomposable, but $(N_0 + cN_\infty)\wedge(N_0 + cN_\infty) = 2c\,N_0\wedge N_\infty$, so $\det A = 0$ and $P(A) = N_0$, forcing $L_A = L_0$ and $A = 0$. Since $\dim \operatorname{Hom}(\Spi,\Som) = 4 = \dim(\Som\wedge\Spi)$, $\varphi$ is an isomorphism.
(3) A $2$-plane $U$ satisfies $U \cap \Som = 0$ if and only if the projection $U \to \Spi$ along $\Som$ is injective, hence bijective, if and only if $U$ is the graph of a unique $A: \Spi \to \Som$; and $U \cap \Som = 0$ is exactly skewness of $\mathbb{P}(U)$ and $L_\infty$. For the quadric statement: for decomposable $P = u_1\wedge u_2$, $\ip{P}{N_\infty} = \varepsilon(u_1\wedge u_2\wedge e_1\wedge e_2)$ vanishes exactly when the four vectors are dependent, i.e.\ when the planes meet; and $\ip{P(A)}{N_\infty} = \varepsilon(N_0\wedge N_\infty) = 1$. Rescaling any quadric point with $\ip{P}{\nInf} \neq 0$ to pairing $1$ places it in the chart, uniquely.
(4) (i) and (ii) are Proposition \claimref{correspondence.skew-lines-splittings-hyperbolic-planes-one} applied to the pair $(\nInf, \nO)$; (iii) is Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(5). (iv): by equivariance of $\Psi$, a spin transformation stabilises the line $L_\infty$ (the plane $\Som$) if and only if it stabilises the ray of the bivector $N_\infty = \Psi(\nInf)$, i.e.\ the ray of $\nInf$ in $V_\C$. That stabiliser is computed in the flat model of \cite{ButlerT6}: the parabolic with Levi factor $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)\oplus\R$ and nilradical the translations, imported here as Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-stabilisers-flat-model} below. The Levi factor preserves both $\Som$ and $\Spi$ (it stabilises both rays), and the assignment of the two $\mathfrak{sl}(2,\C)$ factors of $\mathfrak{so}(1,3)_\C$ to the two planes is Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chiral-planes-summand-spaces}(1). The verification script checks all eleven parabolic basis elements preserve $\Som$, that the complementary four do not, and the chiral assignment itself.

correspondence.local-twistor-transport-a.formal:
Let $\mathcal{T}$ be the tractor bundle of \cite[\S 4]{ButlerT6} and $\CS M$ its spin bundle, the conformal spinor bundle: the rank-four complex bundle with fibre the conformal spinor space $\CS$, carried by the fibrewise Fock model of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra}, associated to a lift of the $SO(2,4)$ tractor bundle to $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$. We assume the conformal manifold is spin, so that the lift exists globally (on the invertible region of a gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime (Definition \claimref{obj.synthesis.gtg-flat-spacetime-gauge-fields}), an open subset of flat spacetime, it does); every statement below is local, and locally a lift always exists. At a point, write $X_p$ for the canonical (tautological) null direction of $\mathcal{T}_p$, and, in a scale, $u_p$ for the null direction with $\ip{X_p}{u_p} = 1$ singled out by the splitting. Then:
\begin{enumerate}
\item the connection of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}(i) decomposes, in the scale, as
\[
\nabla_a \;=\; \nabla^{g}_a \;-\; u_p \wedge e_a \;+\; X_p \wedge \mathrm{P}(e_a),
\]
(for a gravitational field on flat spacetime, with $u_p = \nInf$, $X_p = \nO$ and $e_a = \hb^{-1}(a)$, this is the gauge field $\Omega_{T}(a) = \Omega(a) - \nInf \wedge \hb^{-1}(a) + \nO \wedge \Sch(\hb^{-1}(a))$ of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}, $\nabla^{g}$ being $\Omega(a)$), where $\nabla^g$ couples the Levi factor only: the soldering summand is valued in $u_p\wedge W_\C$ and the Schouten summand in $X_p \wedge W_\C$, with $W_\C = (W_{1,3})_\C$ the complexified Minkowski complement, the latter in the nilradical of the parabolic stabilising $X_p$;
\item on the spinor bundle, with $\Spi$ the plane of $\Psi(X_p)$ (the point's own line: the canonical subbundle) and $\Som$ the plane of $\Psi(u_p)$, the grading element $E := u_p\wedge X_p$ acts with eigenvalue $+\tfrac12$ on $\Som$ and $-\tfrac12$ on $\Spi$; consequently the soldering summand ($E$-weight $+1$) maps $\Spi \to \Som$ and annihilates $\Som$, and the Schouten summand ($E$-weight $-1$) maps $\Som \to \Spi$ and annihilates $\Spi$;
\item the induced spinor connection therefore has, in the scale splitting $Z = (\omega, \pi)$ with $\omega \in \Som$, $\pi \in \Spi$, the form
\[
\nabla^{\CS M}_a(\omega, \pi) = \bigl(\nabla^g_a\omega + \sigma_a\pi,\ \nabla^g_a\pi + \tau_a\omega\bigr),
\]
where $\sigma_a := \rho(-u_p\wedge e_a)|_{\Spi\to\Som}$ is the soldering summand and $\tau_a := \rho(X_p\wedge\mathrm{P}(e_a))|_{\Som\to\Spi}$ the Schouten summand.
The summands are Levi-equivariant in the direction $e_a$, so by Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chiral-planes-summand-spaces}(2) each is the unique map of its type up to a scalar: under Levi-equivariant identifications of $\Som$, $\Spi$ with Penrose's $S^B$, $S_{B'}$, and the \emph{metric-normalised} identification of $W_\C$ with $S^B\otimes S^{B'}$ (the one under which $g_{ab}$ corresponds to $\varepsilon_{AB}\varepsilon_{A'B'}$, Penrose and Rindler's own, fixed up to sign), with $a = AA'$ and $c = CC'$ in the convention of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}(ii), $\sigma_a$ is the $\varepsilon$-contraction $\pi_{A'} \mapsto \varepsilon_A{}^B\pi_{A'}$ times a constant $c_1$ and $\tau_a$ is the Schouten contraction $\omega^B \mapsto \mathrm{P}_{AA'BB'}\omega^B$ times a constant $c_2$. The constants depend on the relative scale of the two spinor identifications, which multiplies $c_1$ by $\lambda$ and $c_2$ by $\lambda^{-1}$ (the sign freedom of the third flips both, so it changes neither their product nor anything not already realised by $\lambda = -1$), so their product is invariant and is fixed by the composite of the summands on $\Som$:
\[
\sigma_a\,\tau_c \;=\; \tfrac12\,c(e_a)\,c(\mathrm{P}(e_c))\big|_{\Som} \;=\; \tfrac12\,\mathrm{P}_{ac}\,\id_{\Som} + \rho\bigl(e_a\wedge\mathrm{P}(e_c)\bigr)\big|_{\Som} .
\]
Penrose's local twistor transport (Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}(ii)) has the same form, with summand composite $\omega^B \mapsto -\varepsilon_A{}^B\,\mathrm{P}_{CC'DA'}\,\omega^D$. Hence Penrose's local twistor bundle is the conformal spinor bundle $\CS M$ and his local twistor transport is the conformal spinor connection, the spinor square root of the tractor connection, exactly when the two composites agree, which is a single convention this identification imports: the sign and normalisation of $\mathrm{P}_{AA'BB'}$ in \cite{PenroseRindler86} relative to the Schouten tensor of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}(i) (Remark \claimref{note.correspondence.one-imported-convention-local-twistor-identification}).
\end{enumerate}
correspondence.local-twistor-transport-a.technical:
On a conformal manifold, assumed spin so that the lift to $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$ exists globally (every statement being local), let $\CS M$ be the rank-four spin bundle of the tractor bundle, with fibre the conformal spinor half $\CS$ of the fibrewise Fock model. In a scale the tractor connection splits as $
abla_a = 
abla^g_a - u_p\wedge e_a + X_p\wedge\mathrm{P}(e_a)$, which for a gravitational field on flat spacetime is the $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field $\Omega(a) - 
Inf\wedge\hb^{-1}(a) + 
O\wedge\mathrm{P}(\hb^{-1}(a))$, a Levi part plus a soldering summand valued in $u_p\wedge W_\C$ and a Schouten summand valued in $X_p\wedge W_\C$, where $X_p$ is the tautological null direction and $u_p$ its partner singled out by the scale. The grading element $E = u_p\wedge X_p$ acts as $+	frac12$ on $\Som$ and $-	frac12$ on $\Spi$, so the soldering summand maps $\Spi	o\Som$, the Schouten summand maps $\Som	o\Spi$, and the induced spinor connection reads $
abla_a(\omega,\pi) = (
abla^g_a\omega + \sigma_a\pi,\ 
abla^g_a\pi + 	au_a\omega)$.

By uniqueness of the equivariant maps, $\sigma_a$ and $	au_a$ are Penrose's $\varepsilon$-contraction and Schouten contraction up to constants $c_1$, $c_2$, whose product is invariant and fixed by the composite $\sigma_a	au_c = 	frac12 c(e_a)c(\mathrm{P}(e_c))|_{\Som}$. Penrose's local twistor transport has the same form, so his local twistor bundle is $\CS M$ and his transport is the conformal spinor connection, the spinor square root of the tractor connection, exactly when the two composites agree, which is a single imported convention: the sign and normalisation of Penrose and Rindler's $\mathrm{P}_{AA'BB'}$ relative to the tractor Schouten tensor.
correspondence.local-twistor-transport-a.lay: Two older formalisms describe the geometry of conformal spacetime: tractors, a six-component bundle with its own connection, and Penrose's four-component bundle with its own transport rule. Assuming the conformal spacetime is spin, so that the tractor bundle has spinors (locally they always exist), this result shows that those spinors, built from the completion's Fock model, carry a connection with exactly the shape of Penrose's transport rule. The two agree completely once one sign and normalisation convention for the curvature term is matched, and that convention is the only thing imported.

proofs.main:
Read in Gauge Theory Gravity: the metric $g$ below is the derived metric of the gravitational field $(\hb, \Omega)$ on flat spacetime, the manifold is the invertible region, and the tractor connection is the flat-space $\Cl(2,4)$ gauge field of Theorem \claimref{synthesis.gtg-tractor-gauge-field-reproduces-tractor-connection}; the index computation below is its reading in the splitting of $g$ (Fact \claimref{synthesis.imported-gtg-dictionary}).

(1) is a computation with the bivector action $(a\wedge b)(v) = \ip{b}{v}a - \ip{a}{v}b$, the action of bivectors on vectors of \claimref{std-algebra.bivector-lie-algebra}, in the splitting $(\sigma, \mu, \rho)$ with $u_p$ the $\sigma$-direction and $X_p$ the $\rho$-direction. The bivector $u_p\wedge e_a$ maps the $\rho$-direction to $-e_a$ and $e_b$ to $g_{ab}\,u_p$, so $-(u_p\wedge e_a)$ contributes $(-\mu_a)$ to the $\sigma$-slot and $(+g_{ab}\rho)$ to the $\mu$-slot; and $(X_p\wedge \mathrm{P}(e_a))$ maps $u_p \mapsto -\mathrm{P}(e_a)$ and $e_b \mapsto \mathrm{P}_{ab}X_p$, contributing $(-\mathrm{P}_{ab}\sigma)$ to the $\mu$-slot and $(+\mathrm{P}_a{}^b\mu_b)$ to the $\rho$-slot. Summing reproduces the display of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}(i) entry by entry. The summand identifications follow: $X_p\wedge W_\C$ annihilates $X_p$, so it lies in the nilradical of the stabiliser of $X_p$ (Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-stabilisers-flat-model} with $X_p$ in place of $\nInf$), while $u_p \wedge W_\C$ moves $X_p$: soldering.
(2) The grading eigenvalues are the two-line Fock computation recorded in the section “The palatial relation: two quantisations, one core” (Proposition \claimref{correspondence.clifford-side-ordering-shift}): $E = u_p\wedge X_p = -(X_p\wedge u_p)$ acts on the module (the Fock model of \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra}) as $\tfrac12 c(u_p)c(X_p) - \tfrac12 = \tfrac12 - N$ with $N$ the occupation number of the $X_p$-mode (the two occupation numbers of a pair sum to one), so with eigenvalue $+\tfrac12$ on the states not containing the $X_p$-mode ($\Som$) and $-\tfrac12$ on those containing it ($\Spi$). For the summands: $[E, u_p\wedge w] = (u_p\wedge w)$ and $[E, X_p\wedge w] = -(X_p\wedge w)$ for $w \in W_\C$ ($E$-weights of $u_p, X_p, w$ are $+1, -1, 0$), so the soldering summand shifts the $E$-grading of spinors by $+1$ and the Schouten summand by $-1$; on a module whose $E$-spectrum is $\{\pm\tfrac12\}$, a weight-$(+1)$ operator maps the $(-\tfrac12)$-space to the $(+\tfrac12)$-space and annihilates the latter, and dually. The verification script confirms both summand actions on all four mixed directions in the Fock model.
(3) The block form is (1) and (2): $\nabla^g$ couples the Levi factor, which preserves both planes, and the two summands are the off-diagonal blocks. Equivariance of the summands: for $\ell$ in the Levi factor, $\ell$ fixes $u_p$ and $X_p$, so $[\rho(\ell), c(u_p)c(e)] = c(u_p)c(\ell e)$ and $[\rho(\ell), c(X_p)c(p)] = c(X_p)c(\ell p)$ by Proposition \claimref{correspondence.spin-representation}; thus $e_a \mapsto \sigma_a$ and $p_c := \mathrm{P}(e_c) \mapsto \tau_c$ are Levi-equivariant maps $W_\C \to \operatorname{Hom}(\Spi,\Som)$ and $W_\C\to\operatorname{Hom}(\Som,\Spi)$, i.e.\ elements of the one-dimensional spaces of Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chiral-planes-summand-spaces}(2), as are Penrose's two contractions; this gives the constants $c_1, c_2$. The composite: with $\rho(u_p\wedge e_a) = \tfrac12 c(u_p)c(e_a)$ and $\rho(X_p\wedge p_c) = \tfrac12 c(X_p)c(p_c)$ (both pairs orthogonal), for $\omega \in \Som$,
\[
\sigma_a\tau_c\,\omega = -\tfrac14\,c(u_p)c(e_a)c(X_p)c(p_c)\,\omega = \tfrac14\,c(u_p)c(X_p)\,c(e_a)c(p_c)\,\omega = \tfrac12\,c(e_a)c(p_c)\,\omega ,
\]
using $c(e_a)c(X_p) = -c(X_p)c(e_a)$, that $c(e_a)c(p_c)$ preserves $\Som$ (it does not involve the $X_p$-mode), and $c(u_p)c(X_p) = 2$ on $\Som$, which is Proposition \claimref{correspondence.clifford-side-ordering-shift} read on the $+\tfrac12$ eigenspace. The decomposition into $\tfrac12\ip{e_a}{p_c}$ and $\rho(e_a\wedge p_c)$ is the definition of $\rho$ on a non-orthogonal pair. The script checks the composite identity on all sixteen pairs of mixed directions. Substituting one summand of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-tractor-connection-local-twistor-transport}(ii) into the other gives Penrose's composite $i\,\varepsilon_A{}^B\,(i\,\mathrm{P}_{CC'DA'}\omega^D) = -\varepsilon_A{}^B\mathrm{P}_{CC'DA'}\omega^D$. Curvature is not needed for the identification and is not used.

correspondence.lorentzian-duality-comple.formal: On $\Lambda^2$ of an oriented $4$-dimensional Lorentzian vector space, the Hodge star satisfies $\ast^2 = -1$; its $\pm i$ eigenspaces $\Lambda^\pm \subset \Lambda^2_\C$ each have dimension three, and complex conjugation (with respect to the real form $\Lambda^2$) interchanges them.
correspondence.lorentzian-duality-comple.technical: On the $2$-forms of an oriented $4$-dimensional Lorentzian vector space the Hodge star satisfies $\ast^2 = -1$, so it is a complex structure on the real six-dimensional space $\Lambda^2$. correspondence.lorentzian-duality-comple.lay: In four-dimensional spacetime the Hodge star sends each plane element to a complementary one. Doing it twice gives minus the original, just as multiplying by the imaginary unit twice gives minus one. So once complex numbers are allowed, the plane elements split into two three-dimensional halves, self-dual and anti-self-dual, which are complex conjugates of each other.

correspondence.one-statement-three-langu.technical:
For a gravitational field on flat spacetime, the infinity bivector of a scale $g$ of its derived metric (Penrose's infinity twistor) is $I_{\alpha\beta} = \Psi(I_g) \in \Lambda^2\CS$, the image under the spinor identification of the scale tractor $I_g = (1, 0, \rho_g)$. On the region of invertibility, vacuum with $\Lambda = 0$ holds if and only if the infinity bivector is covariantly constant for the tractor gauge field $\Omega_{T}$ acting on conformal spinors and simple, a line of $\PCS$ (the infinity line); the Einstein condition with $\Lambda \neq 0$ holds if and only if it is covariantly constant with $\varepsilon(I\wedge I) = \Lambda/3 \neq 0$, a non-simple bivector that is no line at all.

So field equations, tractor parallelism and infinity-bivector constancy are one statement in three languages, and the classical fact that the infinity bivector is simple exactly when $\Lambda = 0$ is the nullity criterion of the spinor identification (null vectors are simple bivectors) applied to the scale tractor.
correspondence.one-statement-three-langu.lay: In this series gravity is a pair of fields on flat spacetime, and Einstein's vacuum equations can be phrased as the statement that one vector of the six-dimensional conformal model, the scale tractor, is constant as those fields carry it around. Translating that object into the spinors of the conformal algebra gives a bivector of that spinor space, the infinity bivector. This result shows that the three formulations say the same thing, and that the familiar fact that this bivector is a genuine line exactly when the cosmological constant vanishes is the same rule that matches lightlike vectors with lines.

correspondence.ordering-filtration.technical:
Grade the palatial algebra $\mathcal{P}$ by total degree in the generators $Z^\alpha$, $\bar Z_\beta$. Two orderings of a monomial of degree at most two differ by an element of $\hbar\,\C$, a central scalar with no tensorial content. Two orderings of a degree-four monomial differ by $\hbar$ times a quadratic plus an element of $\hbar^2\C$; for a balanced monomial, with two $Z$s and two $\bar Z$s, the quadratic is $q(M) + \hbar\C$ with $M \in \mathfrak{gl}(\CS)$, and the discrepancy of $q(M)q(N)$ taken in the two orders is $[q(M), q(N)] = \hbar\,q([M,N])$.

So balanced quartic ordering ambiguities are valued, through $q$, in $\mathfrak{gl}(\CS)$, which contains the conformal algebra $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C \cong \mathfrak{sl}(\CS)$, and quartic order is the first at which an ordering ambiguity can be $\mathfrak{gl}(\CS)$-valued.
correspondence.ordering-filtration.lay: In Penrose's palatial algebra, a noncommutative algebra of operators built on the conformal spinor coordinates, changing the order in which operators are multiplied can change the answer. For products of one or two operators the change is only a fixed number and carries no geometric information. Products of four operators are the first where the change can be a matrix-valued quantity of the same type as the conformal symmetries of spacetime.
correspondence.ordering-filtration.typing_note: Kept the single edge to the symmetrised-quadratics lemma, which the proof uses directly.

proofs.main: Reordering a word is a sequence of adjacent transpositions; transposing $Z^\alpha$ past $\bar Z_\beta$ changes the word by $\hbar\,\delta^\alpha_\beta$ times the word with both letters deleted (the relations; transpositions within the $Z$'s or within the $\bar Z$'s change nothing). (1): for degree $\le 2$ the deleted word is a scalar. (2): for degree $4$ each transposition produces $\hbar$ times a degree-$2$ word, whose own ordering ambiguity is central by (1); deleting one $Z$ and one $\bar Z$ from a balanced word leaves a mixed word $Z^\alpha\bar Z_\beta$, which is $q(E_{\alpha\beta})$ up to a central term by Lemma \claimref{correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-palatial-algebra}(3); the $q$-computation is Lemma \claimref{correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-palatial-algebra}(2). (3): by (1) the quadratic ambiguities are scalars, and degree-$3$ monomials reorder with $\hbar\times$(linear) discrepancies, which are vector-valued, not $\mathfrak{gl}(\CS)$-valued; degree $4$ is the first with a $\mathfrak{gl}(\CS)$-valued discrepancy.

correspondence.reality-conjugation-twist.formal:
Write $v \mapsto \bar v$ for the real structure of $V_\C$ with real points $V$, and $J$ for the antilinear map on $\Lambda^\bullet W$ that conjugates coefficients in the monomial basis built on the isotropic basis of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra}.
\begin{enumerate}
\item (\emph{The conjugation.}) With $\Gamma$ the parity operator ($+1$ on $\CS$, $-1$ on $\CSm$) and $b_4$ the fourth negative basis vector of the section “Setting and imports”,
\[
\kappa := \Gamma\, c(b_4)\, J
\]
is an antilinear bijection of $\Lambda^\bullet W$ with $\kappa\, c(v) = c(\bar v)\, \kappa$ for all $v \in V_\C$; every antilinear map with this property is a complex multiple of $\kappa$; $\kappa$ swaps the chiralities, $\kappa(\CS) = \CSm$; and $\kappa^2 = -\id$.
\item (\emph{The invariant Hermitian form.}) $\Sigma(Z_1, Z_2) := B(\kappa Z_1, Z_2)$ (the twistor form; on the conformal spinor space $\CS$ it corresponds to the reversion form) is a nondegenerate sesquilinear form on $\CS$ with $\Sigma(Z_2, Z_1) = \lambda\,\overline{\Sigma(Z_1, Z_2)}$ for a constant $\lambda$ of modulus one, so that a rescaling of $\kappa$ by a phase makes $\Sigma$ Hermitian; for the $\kappa$ of (1), $\lambda = 1$ and $\Sigma$ is Hermitian as it stands. The real bivectors act $\Sigma$-anti-Hermitianly, so $\Sigma$ is $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$-invariant.
\item (\emph{Null planes.}) For every real null vector $v$ the plane of $\Psi(v)$ is $\Sigma$-null. In particular $\Som$ and $\Spi$ are $\Sigma$-null.
\item (\emph{Signature.}) $\Sigma$ has signature $(2,2)$.
\item (\emph{Reality of the chart, and the factor $I_6$.}) The conformal pseudoscalar $I_6$ acts on $\CS$ as its complex unit (the factor $i$). Let $\sigma(\omega, \pi) := \Sigma(\omega, \pi)$ be the resulting perfect pairing $\Som\times\Spi \to \C$, and call $\hat x: \Spi\to\Som$ \emph{$\sigma$-Hermitian} if $\sigma(\hat x\pi, \pi') = \overline{\sigma(\hat x\pi', \pi)}$ for all $\pi, \pi' \in \Spi$. For $A \in \operatorname{Hom}(\Spi, \Som)$ the following are equivalent: (a) the chart point $m(A)$ of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart} is real, $m(A) \in W_{1,3}$; (b) the line $L_A$ is $\Sigma$-null; (c) $A = I_6\hat x$ with $\hat x$ $\sigma$-Hermitian. Consequently the real points of the affine chart are exactly the $\Sigma$-null lines skew to $L_\infty$, the incidence relation of a real point reads $\omega = I_6\hat x\pi$ with $\hat x$ $\sigma$-Hermitian, and on real points the chart norm is $Q(m) = -2\det A = 2\det\hat x$ in the bases of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart}.
\end{enumerate}
correspondence.reality-conjugation-twist.technical:
There is an antilinear bijection $\kappa = \Gamma\,c(b_4)\,J$ of the Fock module with $\kappa\,c(v) = c(\bar v)\,\kappa$ for all $v \in V_\C$, unique up to a complex multiple; it swaps the chiralities, $\kappa(\CS) = \CSm$, and $\kappa^2 = -\id$. With the Chevalley pairing it gives the invariant Hermitian form $\Sigma(Z_1, Z_2) = B(\kappa Z_1, Z_2)$ on the conformal spinor space $\CS$ (the twistor form, matched to the reversion form): nondegenerate and sesquilinear, Hermitian for this $\kappa$ (and after a phase for any multiple), $\Spin(2,4)$-invariant, and of signature $(2,2)$. For every real null vector $v$ the plane of $\Psi(v)$ is $\Sigma$-null; in particular $\Som$ and $\Spi$ are.

For $A \in \operatorname{Hom}(\Spi, \Som)$ the following are equivalent: the chart point $m(A)$ is real; the line $L_A$ is $\Sigma$-null; and $A = I_6\hat x$, with $I_6$ the complex unit of $\CS$, and $\hat x$ Hermitian for the induced pairing $\sigma$ of $\Som$ with $\Spi$. So the real points of the affine chart are the $\Sigma$-null lines skew to $L_\infty$, the incidence relation of a real point reads $\omega = I_6\hat x\pi$, and there $Q(m) = -2\det A = 2\det\hat x$.
correspondence.reality-conjugation-twist.lay: The spinor space of the conformal algebra, as built here, is a complex space, and real spacetime has to be recovered from it by a reality condition. This result builds that condition from the completion itself: a conjugation operation and, from it, a Hermitian form on the spinor space with two positive and two negative directions. Real spacetime points are exactly the lines of spinors on which this form vanishes, and the complex unit in Penrose's incidence relation, here the conformal pseudoscalar, is forced by this reality condition.
correspondence.reality-conjugation-twist.typing_note: Added the Fock model because the conjugation is built on its monomial basis and uniqueness uses its irreducibility; the incidence edge is a real premise for clause (5) and was kept, the reverse edge having been removed from the incidence theorem.

proofs.main:
(1) In the monomial basis the operators $c(w_j) = \sqrt2\,w_j\wedge$ and $c(w_j') = \sqrt2\,\iota_{w_j'}$ of \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra} have real matrices, so $J c(v) J^{-1} = c(v^\varsigma)$, where $\varsigma$ conjugates the coordinates of $v$ in the isotropic basis. Compare $\varsigma$ with the real structure: $w_1, w_1', w_2, w_2'$ are real vectors, fixed by both, while $\bar w_3 = b_3 - ib_4 = -2w_3'$ and $\bar w_3' = -\tfrac12 w_3$ against $w_3^\varsigma = w_3$, $w_3'^\varsigma = w_3'$. The $\C$-linear map $g$ fixing $w_1, w_1', w_2, w_2'$ and sending $w_3 \mapsto -2w_3'$, $w_3' \mapsto -\tfrac12 w_3$ is the reflection $r$ (\claimref{std-algebra.reflection}, read over $\C$) in $b_4 = -\tfrac{i}{2}(w_3 + 2w_3')$: $r(v) = v - 2\ip{b_4}{v}b_4/Q(b_4) = v + 2\ip{b_4}{v}b_4$ fixes $b_4^\perp \ni w_1, w_1', w_2, w_2'$ and gives $r(w_3) = w_3 - 2i\,b_4 = w_3 - (w_3 + 2w_3') = -2w_3'$. Hence $\bar v = r(v^\varsigma) = (rv)^\varsigma$ for all $v$. In the Clifford algebra, $c(b_4)^{-1} = c(b_4)/Q(b_4) = -c(b_4)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector}) and
\[
c(b_4)\,c(u)\,c(b_4)^{-1} = \bigl(2\ip{b_4}{u} - c(u)c(b_4)\bigr)\bigl(-c(b_4)\bigr) = -2\ip{b_4}{u}c(b_4) - c(u) = -c(ru),
\]
while $\Gamma c(u)\Gamma^{-1} = -c(u)$ because vectors are odd. Therefore
\[
\kappa\,c(v)\,\kappa^{-1} = \Gamma\,c(b_4)\,c(v^\varsigma)\,c(b_4)^{-1}\,\Gamma^{-1} = \Gamma\bigl(-c(r v^\varsigma)\bigr)\Gamma^{-1} = c(r v^\varsigma) = c(\bar v).
\]
Uniqueness: if $\kappa'$ is another antilinear intertwiner, $\kappa^{-1}\kappa'$ is a $\C$-linear operator commuting with $c(V_\C)$ on the irreducible module $\Lambda^\bullet W$; an eigenspace of it is a nonzero submodule, hence everything, so $\kappa^{-1}\kappa'$ is a scalar. Parity: $J$ and $\Gamma$ preserve degree parity and $c(b_4)$ reverses it, so $\kappa(\CS) = \CSm$. The square: $b_4$ has purely imaginary coordinates, so $J c(b_4) J^{-1} = c(b_4^\varsigma) = -c(b_4)$, and with $J^2 = 1$,
\[
\kappa^2 = \Gamma c(b_4)\,\Gamma\,\bigl(J c(b_4) J^{-1}\bigr) = \bigl(-c(b_4)\bigr)\bigl(-c(b_4)\bigr) = c(b_4)^2 = Q(b_4) = -1 .
\]
The script checks the intertwining relation on every basis state for the six basis vectors and their $i$-multiples, the parity swap, and $\kappa^2$.

(2) $\Sigma$ is well defined and nondegenerate: $\kappa$ maps $\CS$ bijectively onto $\CSm$ and $B$ is perfect on $\CSm\times\CS$. Consider $B'(x, y) := \overline{B(\kappa x, \kappa y)}$, a $\C$-bilinear form on $\Lambda^\bullet W$. It vanishes on pairs of equal parity ($\kappa$ swaps parity and $B$ pairs opposite parities only), and every vector is $B'$-self-transpose:
\[
B'(c(v)x, y) = \overline{B(c(\bar v)\kappa x, \kappa y)} = \overline{B(\kappa x, c(\bar v)\kappa y)} = \overline{B(\kappa x, \kappa\, c(v) y)} = B'(x, c(v) y),
\]
by (1) and Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chevalley-pairing}(3). Such forms are unique up to scale: since $B$ is nondegenerate, any bilinear $\beta$ is $\beta(x,y) = B(Tx, y)$ for a unique linear $T$, and if all vectors are self-transpose for both $\beta$ and $B$ then $B(Tc(v)x, y) = \beta(c(v)x, y) = \beta(x, c(v)y) = B(Tx, c(v)y) = B(c(v)Tx, y)$, so $T$ commutes with $c(V_\C)$ and is a scalar by the eigenspace argument of (1). Thus $B' = \lambda_0 B$ for a constant $\lambda_0$, i.e.\ $B(\kappa x, \kappa y) = \bar\lambda_0\,\overline{B(x,y)}$. Applying the construction twice, $\overline{B'(\kappa x, \kappa y)} = B(\kappa^2 x, \kappa^2 y) = B(x, y)$ and also $= \overline{\lambda_0\,B(\kappa x, \kappa y)} = \bar\lambda_0\, B'(x,y) = |\lambda_0|^2 B(x,y)$, so $|\lambda_0| = 1$. Now for $Z_1, Z_2 \in \CS$, using antisymmetry of $B$, $Z_1 = -\kappa^2 Z_1$ and antilinearity of $\kappa$,
\[
\Sigma(Z_2, Z_1) = B(\kappa Z_2, Z_1) = -B(Z_1, \kappa Z_2) = B(\kappa(\kappa Z_1), \kappa Z_2) = \bar\lambda_0\,\overline{B(\kappa Z_1, Z_2)} = \lambda\,\overline{\Sigma(Z_1, Z_2)},
\]
with $\lambda := \bar\lambda_0$.
If $\lambda = e^{i\theta}$, replacing $\kappa$ by $\mu\kappa$ with $\mu := e^{-i\theta/2}$ replaces $\Sigma$ by $\Sigma' = \mu\Sigma$, and $\Sigma'(Z_2,Z_1) = \mu\lambda\,\overline{\Sigma(Z_1,Z_2)} = (\mu\lambda/\bar\mu)\,\overline{\Sigma'(Z_1,Z_2)} = \overline{\Sigma'(Z_1,Z_2)}$, since $\mu\lambda/\bar\mu = e^{-i\theta/2}e^{i\theta}e^{-i\theta/2} = 1$: Hermitian. The script computes $\lambda_0 = \lambda = 1$ for the $\kappa$ of (1) on the full basis, checks that $\Sigma$ is Hermitian and of rank four, and re-runs the relation and the phase on $\kappa$ rescaled by $(3+4i)/5$, where $\lambda \neq 1$. Invariance: for real orthogonal $u, v$ and $\beta = \tfrac12 c(u)c(v)$, (1) gives $\kappa\rho(\beta) = \rho(\beta)\kappa$, so
\[
\Sigma(\rho(\beta)Z_1, Z_2) + \Sigma(Z_1, \rho(\beta)Z_2) = B(\rho(\beta)\kappa Z_1, Z_2) + B(\kappa Z_1, \rho(\beta) Z_2) = 0
\]
by Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chevalley-pairing}(4); the real bivectors span $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$ and exponentiate to $\mathrm{Spin}(2,4)$. The script checks all fifteen.

(3) For a real null $v$ the plane of $\Psi(v)$ is $c(v)\CSm$ (Example \claimref{note.correspondence.isomorphism-witt-pair}), and
\begin{align*}
\Sigma\bigl(c(v)s_1,\, c(v)s_2\bigr) &= B\bigl(\kappa c(v)s_1,\, c(v)s_2\bigr) = B\bigl(c(v)\kappa s_1,\, c(v)s_2\bigr)\\
&= B\bigl(\kappa s_1,\, c(v)^2 s_2\bigr) = Q(v)\,B(\kappa s_1, s_2) = 0 ,
\end{align*}
using $\bar v = v$, Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chevalley-pairing}(3), and nullity. $\Som$ and $\Spi$ are the planes of $\Psi(\nInf)$ and $\Psi(\nO)$, both real and null.

(4) Take bases $e_1, e_2$ of $\Som$ and $\pi_1, \pi_2$ of $\Spi$. By (3) the Gram matrix of the Hermitian form $\Sigma$ on $\CS = \Som\oplus\Spi$ is $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & S \\ S^* & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$ with $S_{ik} := \Sigma(e_i, \pi_k)$, and nondegeneracy forces $S$ to be invertible. Replacing $\pi_1, \pi_2$ by the basis with $S = I$ turns the Gram matrix into $\bigl(\begin{smallmatrix} 0 & I \\ I & 0\end{smallmatrix}\bigr)$, whose eigenvalues are $+1$ and $-1$, each with multiplicity two: signature $(2,2)$. The script reads the signature off $\Sigma$ itself, through its real form.

(5) Here $I_6$, the conformal pseudoscalar, is central in the even algebra and squares to $-1$, so on $\CS$ it acts as the scalar $i$ or $-i$ of the Fock model (the complex unit commuting with the action is forced to be $\pm I_6$, TWGA E1.3d); either sign serves below, since $\hat x$ is $\sigma$-Hermitian exactly when $-\hat x$ is. (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b): if $m(A)$ is real then $P(A) = X(m(A))$ is $\Psi$ of a real null vector, so its plane $L_A$ is $\Sigma$-null by (3). (b) $\Leftrightarrow$ (c): since $\Som$ and $\Spi$ are $\Sigma$-null and $\Sigma$ is Hermitian,
\[
\Sigma(A\pi + \pi,\ A\pi' + \pi') = \Sigma(A\pi, \pi') + \Sigma(\pi, A\pi') = h_A(\pi,\pi') + \overline{h_A(\pi',\pi)}, \qquad h_A(\pi,\pi') := \sigma(A\pi, \pi'),
\]
so $L_A$ is $\Sigma$-null exactly when the sesquilinear form $h_A$ on $\Spi$ is anti-Hermitian. With $\hat x := -I_6A$ and $\sigma$ antilinear in its first slot, $\sigma(\hat x\pi, \pi') = I_6\,h_A(\pi,\pi')$, and $h_A$ is anti-Hermitian exactly when $\sigma(\hat x\pi,\pi') = \overline{\sigma(\hat x\pi',\pi)}$, i.e.\ when $\hat x$ is $\sigma$-Hermitian. (c) $\Rightarrow$ (a): the set $\{A : m(A) \in W_{1,3}\} = \varphi^{-1}(W_{1,3})$ is a real subspace of $\operatorname{Hom}(\Spi,\Som)$ of real dimension four, because $\varphi$ is a $\C$-linear isomorphism onto $(W_{1,3})_\C$ (Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart}(2)); the set $\{I_6\hat x : \hat x\ \sigma\text{-Hermitian}\}$ is likewise a real subspace of real dimension four (Hermitian forms on a $2$-plane); (a) $\Rightarrow$ (b) $\Leftrightarrow$ (c) shows the first is contained in the second, and equal dimensions give equality. The script exhibits four $\sigma$-Hermitian $\hat x$ (the Pauli forms transported through $\sigma$) with $m(i\hat x)$ real and spanning $W_{1,3}$, and checks that $m(\hat x)$ is not real (the script works with the Fock model's scalar $i$, which is $I_6$ up to sign). The consequences: real chart points are the $\Sigma$-null lines skew to $L_\infty$ by (a) $\Leftrightarrow$ (b) and Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart}(3); $\omega = A\pi = I_6\hat x\pi$ with $\hat x$ $\sigma$-Hermitian is Penrose's incidence relation, his Hermitian matrix being $\hat x$ written in bases adapted to $\sigma$ (which rescale $\det$ by a constant, the spin-frame normalisation of Remark \claimref{note.correspondence.what-factor-i-what-remains-conventional}); and in the bases of Theorem \claimref{correspondence.incidence-relation-chart}, $Q(m(A)) = -2\det A = -2\det(I_6\hat x) = 2\det\hat x$ by clause (2) of that theorem, real as it must be.

correspondence.shared-core-ordering-dict.technical:
The symmetrised quadratics of the palatial algebra close under commutator on a copy of $\mathfrak{gl}(\CS) = \mathfrak{gl}(4,\C)$, whose $\Sigma$-anti-Hermitian part is $\mathfrak{u}(2,2)$, containing $\mathfrak{su}(2,2) \cong \mathfrak{so}(2,4)$; the bivectors of $\Cl(2,4)_\C$ close on $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C$ and act on $\CS$ as $\mathfrak{sl}(\CS)$. Under the Klein identification the two copies coincide compatibly with their actions: $\beta \mapsto q(\rho(\beta))/\hbar$ is an injective Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C \to \mathcal{P}$ whose adjoint action on the linear palatial generators is the spinor action $\rho(\beta)$, as $-\rho(\beta)$ on the $Z$ slot and its transpose on the $\bar Z$ slot.

Both quantisations carry the same ordering shift of one half per dimension: on the palatial storey symmetric ordering shifts the distinguished $\mathfrak{u}(1)$ generator by $-\tfrac{\hbar}{2}$ per complex dimension of $\CS$, $-2\hbar$ in all, and on the Clifford storey the boost generator of each adjoined plane is $N - \tfrac12$, minus one half per fermionic mode.
correspondence.shared-core-ordering-dict.lay: Two quite different quantum structures appear in the series: a bosonic algebra of operators on the conformal spinor coordinates, from Penrose's palatial programme, and the fermionic Clifford algebra of the completion. This result shows that, once the two are matched by the Klein identification, both contain the same core, the conformal symmetry algebra of spacetime, acting on the conformal spinors in the same way. Both also show the same offset, minus one half per dimension, which on the palatial side comes from symmetric ordering and on the Clifford side from each fermionic mode.

proofs.main: (1) is Lemma \claimref{correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-palatial-algebra}(2) restricted to the real form: $q$ is defined over any subalgebra of $\mathfrak{gl}(\CS)$, and $M \mapsto q(M)/\hbar$ restricts to $\mathfrak{u}(2,2) := \{M : \Sigma(M\cdot,\cdot) + \Sigma(\cdot,M\cdot) = 0\}$, which has real dimension $16$ and contains its traceless part $\mathfrak{su}(2,2)$; the isomorphism $\mathfrak{su}(2,2)\cong\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$ is Proposition \claimref{correspondence.spin-representation} restricted to the real bivectors, which act $\Sigma$-anti-Hermitianly and trace-free (Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(2)), so that the injective image of the fifteen-dimensional $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)$ is the fifteen-dimensional $\mathfrak{su}(2,2)$. (2) is Proposition \claimref{correspondence.spin-representation}. (3) Compose: $\beta \mapsto \rho(\beta) \in \mathfrak{sl}(\CS) \subset \mathfrak{gl}(\CS) \mapsto q(\rho(\beta))/\hbar$; both maps are injective Lie homomorphisms (Proposition \claimref{correspondence.spin-representation}, Lemma \claimref{correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-palatial-algebra}(2)), and Lemma \claimref{correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-palatial-algebra}(1) says the adjoint action on the generator span is $\rho(\beta)$ again (in the dual pair of slots). (4) is the two cited computations side by side; in words, the conformal algebra is the invariant core of both storeys. The homogeneity dictionary is an identity rather than a convention match: in the realisation $\bar Z_\beta = -\hbar\,\partial_\beta$, the one that satisfies the palatial sign $[Z^\alpha, \bar Z_\beta] = +\hbar\delta^\alpha_\beta$, the generator $q(\mathrm{id})$ acts on homogeneity-$h$ functions as $-(h+2)\hbar$, so eigenfunctions of the helicity operator $s = \tfrac12 q(\mathrm{id})$ with eigenvalue $s\hbar$ have homogeneity exactly $h = -2s - 2$ (the script checks this as an operator identity on all monomials of degree $\le 3$): the $-2$ of Penrose's homogeneity \cite{Penrose1967, PenroseRindler86} \emph{is} the ordering shift of Lemma \claimref{correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-palatial-algebra}(3). This computation is classical: the helicity operator as the symmetrised quadratic $\tfrac14(Z^\alpha\bar Z_\alpha + \bar Z_\alpha Z^\alpha)$ and the resulting $-2s-2$ are Penrose's \cite[Vol.~2, Ch.~6]{PenroseRindler86}; what the series adds is the pairing with the Clifford ordering shift of Proposition \claimref{correspondence.clifford-side-ordering-shift}. The residual freedom (which chirality is called helicity $+s$) is conventional; the magnitude, one half per dimension at each storey, is not.

correspondence.spin-representation.formal:
The bivectors of $\Cl(V_\C)$ close under commutator (a copy of $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C := \Lambda^2 V_\C$, acting on vectors by $[\beta, c(w)] = c(\beta w)$), and their action on the conformal spinor space $\CS$ (twistor space) is a Lie algebra isomorphism
\[
\rho: \mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C \;\xrightarrow{\ \sim\ }\; \mathfrak{sl}(\CS) .
\]
Consequently the image of $\mathrm{Spin}(V_\C)$ in $GL(\CS)$ is all of $SL(\CS)$, which acts transitively on $\CS\setminus\{0\}$.
correspondence.spin-representation.technical: The bivectors of $\Cl(V_\C)$ close under commutator, forming a copy of $\mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C = \Lambda^2 V_\C$ that acts on vectors by $[\beta, c(w)] = c(\beta w)$. Their action on the conformal spinor half $\CS$ is a Lie algebra isomorphism $\rho: \mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C \to \mathfrak{sl}(\CS)$, both sides having dimension fifteen. Consequently the image of $\Spin(V_\C)$ in $GL(\CS)$ is all of $SL(\CS)$, which acts transitively on $\CS\setminus\{0\}$.
correspondence.spin-representation.lay: The conformal symmetries of spacetime, extended to complex numbers, can be realised inside the completed Clifford algebra. Acting on the four-dimensional spinor space of the conformal algebra they give exactly the trace-free linear transformations of that space, no more and no fewer. At the level of groups every volume-preserving linear map of that space is achieved, so any nonzero spinor in it can be moved to any other.

proofs.main: Closure and the vector action: for $\beta = \tfrac12 c(u)c(v) - \tfrac12\ip{u}{v}$, the Clifford relations of $\Cl(V_\C)$ (\claimref{std-algebra.complex-clifford-algebra}(i); \claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares} in the real case) give $[\beta, c(w)] = \ip{v}{w}c(u) - \ip{u}{w}c(v) = c\bigl((u\wedge v)w\bigr)$, so $\operatorname{ad}_\beta$ preserves the space of vectors; for a second such $\beta'= \tfrac12 c(u')c(v') - \tfrac12\ip{u'}{v'}$, the derivation property gives $[\beta, \beta'] = \tfrac12\bigl(c(\beta u')c(v') + c(u')c(\beta v')\bigr)$, a sum of products of two vectors whose scalar parts $\tfrac12(\ip{\beta u'}{v'} + \ip{u'}{\beta v'})$ vanish by the antisymmetry of $\beta$ as a map on $V_\C$: the commutator is again a bivector. The bivectors act on $\CS$ because they are even. Injectivity and trace-freeness of $\rho$ are finite computations, performed exactly by the script: the fifteen basis bivectors have linearly independent, trace-free actions on $\CS$. (Trace-freeness also follows abstractly: closure gives $\rho(\mathfrak{so}) = \rho([\mathfrak{so},\mathfrak{so}]) \subseteq [\mathfrak{gl}(\CS), \mathfrak{gl}(\CS)] = \mathfrak{sl}(\CS)$; the script makes it unconditional.) Since $\dim \mathfrak{so}(2,4)_\C = 15 = \dim\mathfrak{sl}(\CS)$, $\rho$ is an isomorphism. Group level: the image of $\mathrm{Spin}(V_\C)$ is the subgroup of $GL(\CS)$ generated by the exponentials $e^{\rho(\beta)}$, and since $\rho$ is onto $\mathfrak{sl}(\CS)$ and $\mathrm{Spin}(V_\C)$ contains $e^{\beta}$ for every bivector $\beta$, it contains every $e^{tE_{ij}} = 1 + tE_{ij}$ ($i \neq j$); these elementary transvections generate $SL(4,\C)$ (row reduction: any matrix of determinant one is reduced to the identity by them), so the image is all of $SL(\CS)$. Transitivity of $SL(4,\C)$ on nonzero vectors is elementary (extend $u/\lambda$ to a basis of determinant one).

correspondence.spinor-identification.technical:
With $\CS = \Lambda^{\mathrm{even}}W$ from the Fock model, there is a canonical $\Spin$-module isomorphism $\Psi: V_\C \cong \Lambda^2\CS$ under which the quadratic form becomes $P \mapsto \varepsilon(P\wedge P)$ for a fixed volume functional $\varepsilon$ on $\Lambda^4\CS$, so $Q(v) = \varepsilon(\Psi(v)\wedge\Psi(v))$. Hence $v$ is null exactly when $\Psi(v)$ is simple, that is, a $2$-plane of $\CS$ and so a line of $\PCS$.

Consequently the completion's fibre quadric, the space of null rays of $V$, double covers the real slice of the Klein quadric, a ray and its opposite giving one point; those points are the null lines of $V$, and they are lines of $\PCS$.
correspondence.spinor-identification.lay: This result matches the six complex directions of the completed spacetime algebra with the six independent plane elements that can be formed inside the four-dimensional conformal spinor space. Under the match, the lightlike directions are exactly those plane elements that are single planes rather than sums of planes, and in projective terms these are lines of that spinor space. So the lightlike directions of the completion, taken up to sign, are lines in the projective spinor space: the Klein correspondence, obtained from the completion.

proofs.main:
(1) For $v \in V_\C$ define the bilinear form $G_v$ on $\CSm$ by
\[
G_v(s_1, s_2) \;:=\; B\bigl(s_1,\, c(v)\,s_2\bigr), \qquad s_1, s_2 \in \CSm,
\]
which is well defined since $c(v)s_2 \in \CS$ and $B$ pairs $\CSm$ with $\CS$ (Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chevalley-pairing}(1)). $G_v$ is antisymmetric: $G_v(s_2, s_1) = B(s_2, c(v)s_1) = B(c(v)s_2, s_1) = -B(s_1, c(v)s_2) = -G_v(s_1,s_2)$ by clauses (3) and (2) of the lemma. The perfect pairing $B$ identifies $\CSm^{\,*}$ with $\CS$, hence $\Lambda^2(\CSm^{\,*})$ with $\Lambda^2\CS$; let $\Psi(v) \in \Lambda^2\CS$ be the image of $G_v$. The map $\Psi: V_\C \to \Lambda^2\CS$ is linear, and it is injective: if $\Psi(v) = 0$ then $c(v)$ vanishes on $\CSm$ ($B$ is perfect). Choose a non-null $w \perp v$ (the orthogonal complement of $v$ has dimension at least $5$ and a totally null subspace has dimension at most $3$). For $s \in \CSm$, $c(v)c(w)s = 2\ip{v}{w}s - c(w)c(v)s = 0$ (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}), and $c(w): \CSm \to \CS$ is bijective because $c(w)^2 = Q(w) \neq 0$ (\claimref{std-algebra.inverse-of-vector}); so $c(v)$ vanishes on $\CS$ as well, $c(v) = 0$, and $v = 0$ by injectivity of $c$ (Theorem \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra}). Since $\dim_\C \Lambda^2\CS = \binom42 = 6 = \dim_\C V_\C$, $\Psi$ is an isomorphism. Equivariance: $\mathrm{Spin}$ acts on $c(v)$ by conjugation, giving $c(gv)$, and on $G_v$ through its module actions; $B$ is invariant (Lemma \claimref{correspondence.chevalley-pairing}(4)), so $\Psi(gv) = g\,\Psi(v)$ with the induced action on $\Lambda^2\CS$. The form: $(v, v') \mapsto \varepsilon_0(\Psi(v)\wedge\Psi(v'))$, with $\varepsilon_0$ any generator of $(\Lambda^4\CS)^*$, is a symmetric $\mathrm{Spin}$-invariant bilinear form on $V_\C$, hence proportional to $\ip{\cdot}{\cdot}$ (the space of invariant symmetric forms on the irreducible $V_\C$ is one-dimensional: an invariant form is $\ip{T\cdot}{\cdot}$ for a $T$ commuting with the action, hence a scalar by Schur; and $V_\C$ is irreducible under $\mathfrak{so}(V_\C)$, since for an invariant $U \ni v \neq 0$ with $v_j := \ip{e_j}{v} \neq 0$ in an orthonormal basis, $(e_k\wedge e_i)(e_i\wedge e_j)v = Q(e_i)\,v_j\,e_k$ for distinct $i, j, k$ and $(e_j\wedge e_k)e_k = Q(e_k)\,e_j$, nonzero multiples in either case, so $U = V_\C$). The constant is not zero and is computed in the standard bases: with $\CS$-basis $t_0 = 1$, $t_1 = w_2\wedge w_3$, $t_2 = w_3 \wedge w_1$, $t_3 = w_1\wedge w_2$, $\CSm$-basis $(w_1, w_2, w_3, w_{123})$, and $\varepsilon_0(t_0\wedge t_1\wedge t_2\wedge t_3) = 1$, a direct computation (printed in the script, and in Example \claimref{note.correspondence.isomorphism-witt-pair} below) gives $\Psi(w_1) = -\sqrt2\; t_2\wedge t_3$ and $\Psi(w_1') = \sqrt2\; t_0 \wedge t_1$, whence $\varepsilon_0(\Psi(w_1)\wedge\Psi(w_1')) = -2 = -2\ip{w_1}{w_1'}$. Setting $\varepsilon := -\tfrac12\,\varepsilon_0$ gives $\varepsilon(\Psi(v)\wedge\Psi(v')) = \ip{v}{v'}$ exactly, which the script confirms on all twenty-one basis pairs.
(2) A bivector $P \in \Lambda^2\CS$ on a four-dimensional space is decomposable if and only if $P \wedge P = 0$: decomposable implies $s\wedge t\wedge s\wedge t = 0$; conversely, an antisymmetric bilinear form on $\CS^*$ has a basis in which it reads $t_0\wedge t_1$ or $t_0\wedge t_1 + t_2\wedge t_3$ (pick $t_0, t_1$ with $P(t_0,t_1) = 1$ and repeat on their $P$-orthogonal complement), and in the second case $P\wedge P = 2\,t_0\wedge t_1\wedge t_2\wedge t_3 \neq 0$; in coordinates $P\wedge P = 2\,\mathrm{Pf}(P)\, t_0\wedge t_1\wedge t_2 \wedge t_3$ with $\mathrm{Pf}$ the Pfaffian, which the script uses. By (1), $Q(v) = \varepsilon(\Psi(v)\wedge\Psi(v))$, so $v$ is null iff $\Psi(v)\wedge\Psi(v) = 0$ iff $\Psi(v)$ is simple, i.e.\ represents a $2$-plane of $\CS$, i.e.\ a line of $\PCS$.
(3) The fibre quadric (\claimref{correspondence.imported-forced-completion-fibre-quadric}) is the space of null rays of the real slice $V \subset V_\C$; each null ray spans a complex null line, hence by (2) a point of the Klein quadric $\{[P] : P\wedge P = 0\} \subset \mathbb{P}(\Lambda^2\CS)$, i.e.\ a line of $\PCS$. The assignment factors through the null lines of $V$ (a ray and its opposite span the same complex line) and is injective on them. Which lines of $\PCS$ arise from real points is a reality condition, settled in Proposition \claimref{correspondence.reality-conjugation-twistor-form-factor}(5).

correspondence.statistics-no-go.formal: The palatial algebra admits no nonzero finite-dimensional representation, and no embedding of unital algebras into any finite-dimensional algebra; in particular none into $\Cl(2,4)$ or $\Cl(2,4)_\C$, of dimension $64$.
correspondence.statistics-no-go.technical: The palatial algebra, whose generators obey canonical commutation relations $[Z^\alpha, \bar Z_\beta] = \hbar\,\delta^\alpha_\beta$, has no nonzero finite-dimensional representation and admits no embedding of unital algebras into any finite-dimensional algebra. In particular it cannot sit inside $\Cl(2,4)$ or $\Cl(2,4)_\C$, each of dimension $64$.
correspondence.statistics-no-go.lay: Penrose's palatial programme uses operators obeying the same kind of commutation rule as position and momentum in quantum mechanics. Such operators can never be written as finite matrices. So the palatial algebra cannot be placed inside the completion's Clifford algebra, which has only sixty-four dimensions.
correspondence.statistics-no-go.typing_note: Removed the ladder-pairs fact: the proof cites it only in the closing contrast with the fermionic side, and the trace argument does not use it.

proofs.main: In a representation on a nonzero finite-dimensional space $U$, take the trace of $[Z^1, \bar Z_1] = \hbar\,\mathrm{id}_U$: the left side has trace zero (the trace of any commutator of endomorphisms), the right side $\hbar\dim U \neq 0$. For the embedding statement: a unital embedding $\mathcal{P} \hookrightarrow A$ into a finite-dimensional algebra composes with the left regular representation of $A$ to give a finite-dimensional faithful representation of $\mathcal{P}$, which does not exist. The contrast with the fermionic side is instructive and exact: the CAR relation $ff^* + f^*f = 1$ is an \emph{anti}commutator, to which the trace argument does not apply, and indeed the ladder pairs lie in the $64$-dimensional $\Cl(2,4)$ (Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-ladder-pairs-fock-modules-over}). Bose statistics forbids finite dimensions; Fermi statistics is built from them.

correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-pa.technical:
For $M \in \mathfrak{gl}(4,\C)$ the symmetrised quadratic $q(M) = \tfrac12\sum M^\beta{}_\alpha(Z^\alpha\bar Z_\beta + \bar Z_\beta Z^\alpha)$ in the palatial algebra $\mathcal{P}$ acts on the linear generators as $M$ times $\hbar$: $[q(M), Z^\gamma] = -\hbar\,(MZ)^\gamma$ and $[q(M), \bar Z_\gamma] = \hbar\,(M^{\mathsf T}\bar Z)_\gamma$. Moreover $[q(M), q(N)] = \hbar\,q([M,N])$, so $M \mapsto q(M)/\hbar$ is an injective Lie algebra homomorphism $\mathfrak{gl}(4,\C) \to \mathcal{P}$.

Symmetric and normal orderings differ by a central term, $q(M) = \sum M^\beta{}_\alpha Z^\alpha\bar Z_\beta - \tfrac{\hbar}{2}\operatorname{tr}M$; for the distinguished generator $M = \id$, the helicity or homogeneity direction, the shift is $-2\hbar$, minus one half of $\hbar$ for each of the four complex dimensions of the conformal spinor space.
correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-pa.lay: In the palatial algebra, whose generators are the four coordinates of a conformal spinor and their conjugates promoted to operators, one can build quadratic combinations of generators, averaged over the two possible orders. These combinations reproduce the algebra of four-by-four complex matrices, acting on the generators just as matrices act on vectors. Averaging the order, instead of always putting one kind of operator first, shifts each combination by a fixed number, which for the generator tied to helicity is minus one half for each of the four dimensions of the spinor space.
correspondence.symmetrised-quadratics-pa.typing_note: No edges; the symmetrised-quadratic computation is classical (Penrose and Rindler) but no imported claim for it is in the store, so no standard route.

proofs.main:
(1) $[Z^\alpha\bar Z_\beta, Z^\gamma] = Z^\alpha[\bar Z_\beta, Z^\gamma] = -\hbar\,\delta^\gamma_\beta Z^\alpha$, and the same for the reversed ordering, so $[q(M), Z^\gamma] = -\hbar\sum_\alpha M^\gamma{}_\alpha Z^\alpha$; likewise $[Z^\alpha \bar Z_\beta, \bar Z_\gamma] = \hbar\,\delta^\alpha_\gamma\,\bar Z_\beta$ gives the second display.
(2) $\operatorname{ad}_{q(M)}$ is a derivation, so by (1),
\[
[q(M), q(N)] = \tfrac12\sum N^\beta{}_\alpha\Bigl(\,[q(M),Z^\alpha]\bar Z_\beta + Z^\alpha[q(M),\bar Z_\beta] + [q(M),\bar Z_\beta]Z^\alpha + \bar Z_\beta[q(M),Z^\alpha]\Bigr),
\]
and collecting coefficients of the symmetrised monomials gives $-\hbar\,q(NM) + \hbar\,q(MN) = \hbar\,q([M,N])$. Injectivity: the adjoint action (1) recovers $M$. The verification script confirms (2) in the polynomial realisation $Z^\alpha = z_\alpha$, $\bar Z_\beta = -\hbar\,\partial_\beta$ (the sign that realises $[Z^\alpha, \bar Z_\beta] = +\hbar\delta^\alpha_\beta$, checked as an operator identity), where both sides are operators determined by their action on polynomials of degree $\le 2$, checked exactly on that finite basis.
(3) $\bar Z_\beta Z^\alpha = Z^\alpha \bar Z_\beta - \hbar\delta^\alpha_\beta$, so $\tfrac12(Z^\alpha\bar Z_\beta + \bar Z_\beta Z^\alpha) = Z^\alpha\bar Z_\beta - \tfrac{\hbar}{2}\delta^\alpha_\beta$; summing against $M$ gives the display, and $\operatorname{tr}(\mathrm{id}) = 4$ gives the shift $-2\hbar$, $q(\mathrm{id}) = \sum_\alpha Z^\alpha\bar Z_\alpha - 2\hbar$.

correspondence.twistors-are-states-three.technical:
For a nonzero conformal spinor $u \in \CS$, the annihilator $W_u = \{v \in V_\C : c(v)u = 0\}$ is a maximal totally isotropic, three-dimensional subspace of the complexified ambient space, so every conformal spinor is a pure spinor. The joint kernel of $c(W_u)$ is the line $\C u$, so $[u] \mapsto W_u$ embeds $\PCS$ into the maximal isotropic subspaces, equivariantly for the spin action.

For any isotropic complement $U'$ dual to $W_u$, the map $\Lambda^\bullet U' \to \Lambda^\bullet W$, $\xi \mapsto c(\xi)u$, is a linear isomorphism: $u$ is the Fock vacuum of the three fermionic ladder pairs built on $(W_u, U')$, with even products generating $\CS$ and odd ones $\CSm$. Ambient vectors act as sums of three creation and annihilation operators, so conformal spinors are states of the pair algebra rather than its operators, and no maximal isotropic subspace annihilates both a nonzero even and a nonzero odd spinor.
correspondence.twistors-are-states-three.lay: The four-component spinors of the conformal algebra are the objects Penrose built his theory on. This result shows that, inside the completed algebra of the series, each such spinor is the empty state (the vacuum) of a system of three fermionic ladder pairs that the spinor itself singles out. Every other state of the module is reached from it by those ladder operators, so these spinors are the states the operators act on, not the operators themselves.
correspondence.twistors-are-states-three.typing_note: All three uses are proof premises (transitivity from the spin representation, irreducibility from the Fock model, the ladder-pair normalisation from the imported fact); the paper's remark calls clause (1) classical (Cartan, Chevalley), but that covers one clause only, so no standard-route derivation was added although the Cartan purity import is in the store.

proofs.main:
(1) Isotropy is general: $v \in W_u$ gives $Q(v)u = c(v)^2u = 0$, and $v_1, v_2 \in W_u$ give $2\ip{v_1}{v_2}u = \{c(v_1), c(v_2)\}u = 0$ (\claimref{std-algebra.vector-squares}), so $W_u$ is totally isotropic, hence contained in its own orthogonal complement, so $2\dim W_u \le 6$ and $\dim W_u \le 3$. For the vacuum $u_0 = 1 \in \Lambda^0 W$: $c(w')1 = 0$ for $w' \in W'$ and $c(w+w')1 = \sqrt2\,w$, so $W_{u_0} = W'$, of dimension exactly $3$. By Proposition \claimref{correspondence.spin-representation} the spin image acts transitively on $\CS\setminus\{0\}$, and the construction is equivariant, $W_{gu} = g(W_u)$ (from $c(gv) = g c(v) g^{-1}$), so $\dim W_u = 3$ for every $u \neq 0$. Joint kernel: for $W_{u_0} = W'$ the joint kernel of the three contractions $\iota_{w'}$ is $\Lambda^0 W = \C\cdot 1$ (if $x$ has a nonzero component on a monomial $w_S$ with $S \neq \emptyset$, pick any $i \in S$: the $w_{S\setminus i}$-component of $\iota_{w_i'}x$ comes from $w_S$ alone, since $\iota_{w_i'}w_{S'} = \pm w_{S'\setminus i}$ or $0$ and $S'\setminus i = S\setminus i$ with $i \in S'$ forces $S' = S$, so it is nonzero); equivariance transports the statement to every $u$.
(2) The image $c\bigl(\Lambda^\bullet U'\bigr)u$ equals $c(\Cl(V_\C))u$: the anticommutation relations reorder any word in the basis vectors of $U' \oplus W_u$ into a combination of normally ordered products $c(\xi')c(\eta)$ with $\xi'$ a monomial in $U'$ and $\eta$ a monomial in $W_u$, so these $8\cdot 8 = 64$ products span $\Cl(V_\C)$ (the spanning half of \claimref{std-algebra.blade-basis}, over $\C$); acting on $u$, the right-hand factor $c(\eta)$ gives $0$ unless $\eta = 1$, since $c(W_u)u = 0$; $c(\Cl(V_\C))u$ is a nonzero submodule, hence everything, by irreducibility (Theorem \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra}). So the map is surjective from a space of dimension $2^3 = 8$ onto a space of dimension $8$, hence bijective. The parity statement holds because $c(\xi)$ for even (odd) $\xi$ preserves (swaps) the chirality halves and $u$ is even; if $u \in \CSm$ instead, the roles swap. Normalising a basis of $W_u$ against the dual basis of $U'$ produces three pairs with $f^2 = f^{*2} = 0$, $ff^* + f^*f = 1$: the ladder pairs of Fact \claimref{correspondence.imported-ladder-pairs-fock-modules-over}, here over $\C$; the script checks all CAR relations exactly. Complements dual to $W_u$ exist: for a basis $w_1, w_2, w_3$ of $W_u$ choose $v_j$ with $\ip{w_i}{v_j} = \delta_{ij}$ (the functionals $\ip{w_i}{\cdot}$ are independent) and set $u_j := v_j - \tfrac12\sum_k \ip{v_j}{v_k}\,w_k$; then $\ip{w_i}{u_j} = \delta_{ij}$ and $\ip{u_j}{u_k} = \ip{v_j}{v_k} - \tfrac12\ip{v_k}{v_j} - \tfrac12\ip{v_j}{v_k} = 0$, so $U' := \operatorname{span}(u_j)$ is a dual isotropic complement. Nothing below depends on the choice.
(3) The first sentence is Theorem \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra} read through (2): a vector $v = w + w'$ acts as a creation operator plus an annihilation operator of the $u$-adapted system. Disjointness: if $U = W_{u} = W_{u'}$ with $u \in \CS\setminus 0$, $u' \in \CSm\setminus 0$, the joint kernel of $c(U)$ would contain the two-dimensional space $\C u \oplus \C u'$, contradicting (1).

lepton.imported-twistor-state-pair-syste.formal: Let $W$ be a maximal isotropic subspace of the complexified ambient space $V_{\C}$ of the completion $\Cl(2,4)$. The complexified ascended algebra acts irreducibly on the eight-dimensional Dirac module $\Sp := \Lambda^{\bullet}W$, whose chirality halves are $\CS = \Lambda^{\mathrm{even}}W$ and $\CSm = \Lambda^{\mathrm{odd}}W$. Every nonzero conformal spinor (twistor) $u \in \CS$ is the Fock vacuum of the three fermionic ladder pairs built on its annihilator space $W_{u}$, and for any maximal isotropic complement $U'$ dual to $W_u$ the map $\Lambda^{\bullet}U' \to \Sp$, $\xi \mapsto c(\xi)u$, is a linear isomorphism: every state of the module is generated from $u$ by its own pair operators, the even products landing in $\CS$ and the odd ones in $\CSm$. Conformal spinors are states of the pair algebra, not its operators. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~3.1, 5.3]{ButlerT9}; \cite[Fact~2.2]{ButlerT12}.
lepton.imported-twistor-state-pair-syste.technical:
Let $W$ be a maximal isotropic subspace of $V_\C$ for the completion $\Cl(2,4)$. The complexified ascended algebra acts irreducibly on the eight-dimensional Dirac module $\Sp = \Lambda^\bullet W$, whose chirality halves are $\CS = \Lambda^{\mathrm{even}}W$ and $\CSm = \Lambda^{\mathrm{odd}}W$.

Each nonzero conformal spinor $u \in \CS$ is the Fock vacuum of the three ladder pairs built on its annihilator $W_u$, and for any maximal isotropic complement $U'$ dual to $W_u$ the map $\xi \mapsto c(\xi)u$ is a linear isomorphism $\Lambda^\bullet U' \to \Sp$, even products landing in $\CS$ and odd ones in $\CSm$. This restates earlier results of the series for use in the lepton setting.
lepton.imported-twistor-state-pair-syste.lay: This restates earlier results of the series. A four-component spinor of the conformal algebra is the empty state of its own small system of fermionic ladder operators, and applying those operators to it produces every state of the eight-dimensional Dirac module. These spinors are therefore states, not operators.

proofs.main: Let $W$ be a maximal isotropic subspace of the complexified ambient space $V_{\C}$ of the completion $\Cl(2,4)$, with a dual isotropic complement $U'$. The complexified ascended algebra acts irreducibly on the eight-dimensional Dirac module $\Sp := \Lambda^{\bullet}W$, whose chirality halves are $\CS = \Lambda^{\mathrm{even}}W$ and $\CSm = \Lambda^{\mathrm{odd}}W$. Every nonzero conformal spinor (twistor) $u \in \CS$ is the Fock vacuum of the three fermionic ladder pairs built on its annihilator space $W_{u}$, and the map $\Lambda^{\bullet}U' \to \Sp$, $\xi \mapsto c(\xi)u$, is a linear isomorphism: every state of the module is generated from $u$ by its own pair operators, the even products landing in $\CS$ and the odd ones in $\CSm$. Conformal spinors are states of the pair algebra, not its operators. \emph{Provenance:} \cite[Thms.~3.1, 5.3]{ButlerT9} (\claimref{correspondence.twistors-are-states-three-ladder-pairs}, \claimref{correspondence.fock-model-complexified-ascended-algebra}); \cite[Fact~2.2]{ButlerT12} (\claimref{standard-model.imported-pair-systems-two-chirality-halves}).
